questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that the opening stock of a business is 6,000,000 Frs. Purchases were 2,000,000 Frs. closing stock are 3,000,000 Frs. and net sales are 8,000,000 Frs. Calculate:

i) Cost of goods sold.

ii) Gross profits

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The cost of goods sold and the gross profit come from the **trading account**. (All amounts are in francs, written Frs, as in the question.)

**i) Cost of goods sold**

Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases - Closing stock

= 6,000,000 + 2,000,000 - 3,000,000

Goods available for sale = 6,000,000 + 2,000,000 = 8,000,000 Frs

**Cost of goods sold = 8,000,000 - 3,000,000 = 5,000,000 Frs**

**ii) Gross profit**

Gross profit = Net sales - Cost of goods sold

= 8,000,000 - 5,000,000

**Gross profit = 3,000,000 Frs**

**Trading account (summary)**

| Item | Frs |
|---|---:|
| Net sales | 8,000,000 |
| Opening stock | 6,000,000 |
| Add purchases | 2,000,000 |
| Goods available for sale | 8,000,000 |
| Less closing stock | (3,000,000) |
| Cost of goods sold | (5,000,000) |
| **Gross profit** | **3,000,000** |

**Check.** Gross profit as a percentage of sales = 3,000,000 / 8,000,000 x 100 = 37.5 %, and the mark-up on cost = 3,000,000 / 5,000,000 x 100 = 60 % (these two figures are extra and are not asked).

**Answers: (i) cost of goods sold = 5,000,000 Frs; (ii) gross profit = 3,000,000 Frs.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain FOUR reasons why profits are important to a business.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Profit is the surplus left when the total costs of a business are taken from its total revenue. It is the main aim of most businesses, and it is important for the following reasons.

1. **It is the reward of the owner for his work and risk.** Profit is the income of the owner (or the dividend of the shareholders); without it, the owner has no reason to continue the business.

2. **It is a source of finance for expansion.** Profit that is kept in the business (ploughed back) is used to buy new machines, open new branches or increase stock, without borrowing and without paying interest.

3. **It ensures the survival of the business.** A business that makes profit can pay its debts, wages and other costs, and can face bad periods or competition. A business that keeps making losses closes down.

4. **It attracts investors and lenders.** Banks and investors are ready to lend money or buy shares in a profitable business, which makes it easy to raise capital.

5. **It measures efficiency and helps the government.** A good profit shows that the business is well managed, and it brings tax revenue to the government and allows the business to pay good wages.

**Conclusion.** Profit is the life-blood of a business: it rewards the owner, finances growth and keeps the firm in operation.

questions.enonce_markdown:
With the use of TWO examples explain the following;

i) Current assets

ii) Current liabilities.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**i) Current assets.** These are the **assets of a business which are held for a short time and which are used up or changed into cash within one year (in the normal course of business)**. They change constantly. *Two examples:* **stock** (goods for sale, worth 3,000,000 Frs for instance) and **debtors** (customers who owe the business money for goods bought on credit). Other examples are cash in hand and cash at bank.

**ii) Current liabilities.** These are the **debts of a business which must be paid within one year**. *Two examples:* **creditors** (suppliers to whom the business owes money for goods bought on credit) and a **bank overdraft** (money owed to the bank for a short time). Other examples are accrued expenses (wages or rent not yet paid) and tax due.

**Conclusion.** Current assets less current liabilities gives the **working capital**, which shows whether the business can pay its short-term debts.
